title: One Fact Changes Everything — Drift
blurb: Two near-identical incidents. One fact differs, and the diagnosis flips.
source: Gama et al. (2014), A survey on concept drift adaptation · Moreno-Torres et al. (2012), A unifying view on dataset shift

pairs.dimension: whether the input-to-outcome relationship still holds

a.text: A credit model sees a wave of applicants from a new region. For any given income, employment and history profile, default rates are exactly what the model expects.
a.why: The inputs moved into new territory but the rule is intact. More representative training data fixes it; a new rule is not needed.

b.text: A credit model sees the same wave of applicants from a new region. For an identical income, employment and history profile, default rates there are twice what the model expects.
b.why: Identical inputs now produce different outcomes, so P(Y|X) has changed. No amount of rebalancing the input mix will fix a relationship that no longer holds.

pairs.dimension: whether the change originates in the world or in the pipeline

a.text: A pricing model's error jumps on a Tuesday. Investigation finds a competitor launched an aggressive discount campaign that morning.
a.why: A real change in the world altered the relationship the model encodes. Retraining on post-change data is the correct response.

b.text: A pricing model's error jumps on a Tuesday. Investigation finds the overnight ETL job began writing list price into the field that previously held net price.
b.why: Nothing about pricing behaviour changed — the model is being fed a different quantity under the same name. Retraining here bakes the defect in and hides it.

pairs.dimension: whether the old and new regimes coexist during the transition

a.text: Over six months a fraud model degrades as an old attack pattern is progressively replaced by a new one. Throughout the period, both patterns arrive in volume.
a.why: Two distinct concepts overlapping in time, with the mixture weight moving. An ensemble that keeps a model per concept handles this well.

b.text: Over six months a fraud model degrades as attackers continuously adjust transaction sizes upward in small steps, with no distinct old and new pattern at any point.
b.why: One concept moving smoothly through intermediate states. A rolling retraining window tracks it; concept-switching machinery has nothing to switch between.

pairs.dimension: whether the shift is in the inputs or in the outcome mix

a.text: A screening model is deployed at a new clinic. The patients are younger and fitter than the training population, and disease prevalence is unchanged.
a.why: The feature distribution moved while the outcome mix did not. The concern is extrapolation into thinly-covered input regions.

b.text: A screening model is deployed at a new clinic. The patients look demographically identical to the training population, but disease prevalence is a quarter of what it was.
b.why: P(Y) moved with P(X|Y) intact, so the model's ranking still works but its probabilities are systematically too high. Prior correction, not retraining.

pairs.dimension: whether ground-truth labels are available to confirm the degradation

a.text: A collections model's share of high-risk scores rises from 12% to 25% in a month. Outcomes take ninety days to observe, so none are yet available for this cohort.
a.why: An output-distribution change with no labels is a signal to investigate, not a finding. It may be a correct response to a genuinely riskier population.

b.text: A collections model's share of high-risk scores rises from 12% to 25% in a month, and the cohort from ninety days ago has now resolved with precision down 18 points.
b.why: Labels have arrived and quality has actually fallen. Only now is retraining justified on evidence rather than on the shape of a histogram.

a.text: A logistics model's accuracy collapses every year in the fortnight before Christmas and recovers immediately afterwards.
a.why: A known concept that comes back on a cycle. Retire nothing: keep the seasonal model and select it by context.

b.text: A logistics model's accuracy collapses in the fortnight after a permanent change to national delivery regulations, and never recovers.
b.why: An abrupt, one-way change with no return. The pre-change model has no further use and the pre-change data has limited value for retraining.

pairs.dimension: whether the target definition or the population changed

a.text: A moderation team rewrites its guidance so that a category of borderline content is now labelled 'violating' where it was previously 'acceptable'. The content arriving is unchanged.
a.why: Same inputs, different labels: the mapping was redefined. Every historical label under the old guidance is now partly wrong for training purposes.

b.text: A moderation team's guidance is unchanged, but a viral trend means genuinely violating content rises from 2% to 9% of the queue.
b.why: The rule is stable; the mix of outcomes moved. Thresholds and capacity planning need attention, not the model's learned boundary.

pairs.dimension: whether the monitored change is in the model or in the data

a.text: Scores shift the day a new model version is released. A fixed reference sample, replayed through both versions, reproduces the shift exactly.
a.why: Identical inputs producing different outputs isolates the change to the model. This is the expected use of a golden reference sample at release.

b.text: Scores shift the day a new model version is released. The same fixed reference sample, replayed through both versions, produces identical outputs.
b.why: If the model is provably unchanged on fixed inputs, the live inputs must have changed — and a same-day coincidence points at the deploy's data-side changes, not at the world.
